newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope urges reconciliation in war-scarred Beirut.
newsitem.headline: Pope urges reconciliation in war-scarred Beirut.

text.p: Pope John Paul, given a tumultuous welcome on the first day of his visit to Lebanon, on Sunday takes his message of Moslem-Christian reconciliation into the battle-scarred heart of Beirut.
Tens of thousands of people were expected at an open-air mass on a seafront esplanade beside the former Green Line battlefront where Moslem and Christian militias fought during the 1975-90 civil war.
The mass is the central event of John Paul's 32-hour visit, his first trip to the Middle East, which ends on Sunday evening.

The Pope will issue a document entitled "A New Hope for Lebanon" summing up the conclusions of a 1995 Vatican synod of the Lebanese church which will be closely watched by Moslems as well as Christians.

Lebanon's bishops, in their own conclusions issued after the synod, called for the withdrawal of Syrian and Israeli troops from Lebanon and denounced what they saw as the isolation of the Christian minority in postwar Lebanon.

The call caused an uproar among Moslems who sent an envoy to the Vatican to discuss it. Moslem political and spiritual leaders are concerned over the extent to which the pope's document may echo the bishops' views.
The Pope began his visit on Saturday by calling on the Lebanese to break down the barriers of mistrust erected by civil war and build a society open to Christians and Moslems alike.

He also issued a veiled call, without mentioning the two countries by name, for the withdrawal of the 35,000 Syrian troops stationed in Lebanon and 2,000 Israeli troops who hold a southern border strip that comprises more than 10 percent of the country's territory.
Big crowds, particularly in Christian areas, greeted the Pope as he drove through Beirut, showering his bulletproof Popemobile with rice and rose petals and releasing doves in its path.

Some 20,000 cheering, clapping, whistling, chanting young people later gave the 76-year-old pontiff a reception worthy of a rock star at an evening meeting at Harissa, Lebanon's main Marian shrine north of Beirut.
"John Paul Two, we love you," and "Long Live Peace" they chanted, repeatedly applauding the Pope in one of the warmest receptions he has received during his travels in recent years.

They also asked John Paul for help. Student Pierre Najm told him in a speech that many young Lebanese had lost faith in politics, religion and their country amid a loss of fundamental freedoms under pro-Syrian governments since the civil war.
"We ask you...to dare to say out loud the things which we are afraid to say...Be our courage and call things by their name," Najm said.
The Pope replied that the youth of Lebanon should not build new barriers within their country.
"I understand the aspirations which drive you and your impatience before the daily situation which you seem unable to change," he said.
"Do not build new walls in the bosom of your country.
"Your task is to build bridges between people, between families and between the different communities." he said.
"You must also ensure that each Lebanese, especially the young, may take part in the life of society, in the common home," the Pope added.

But Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, patriarch of the Maronite church, drew huge applause and chants of "Freedom, freedom" when he told the Pope that young Lebanese demanding democracy, human rights and justice were barred from political advancement under the postwar government.
